           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                       )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                         )
         FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                            )
         APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA-LARGE LOAD                        )
         TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                        )     CASE NO. PUD2026-000046
         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                              )
         CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                       )
         RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                             )
         PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                           )


                 RESPONSE OF THE PUBLIC UTILITY DIVISION IN OBJECTION TO
              OG&E’S MOTION TO AMEND THE PROCEDURAL SCHEDULE IN ORDER
                  NO. 758969 TO INCLUDE A BRIEFING SCHEDULE REGARDING
               PROPOSALS FOR ALTERNATIVE ELECTRIC SERVICE FRAMEWORKS

                COMES NOW the Public Utility Division (“PUD”) of the Oklahoma Corporation

         Commission (“Commission”), by and through its undersigned counsel, and respectfully objects to

         OG&E’s Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in Order No. 758969 to Include a Briefing

         Schedule Regarding Proposals for Alternative Electric Service Frameworks (“Motion”), filed by

         Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) on September 22, 2026 (Entry

         No. 45). For the reasons set forth below, PUD requests that the Administrative Law Judge (“ALJ”)

         deny the Motion. In support of its objection, PUD states as follows:


                                        I. SUMMARY OF OBJECTION

                The Motion asks the ALJ to amend a negotiated procedural schedule, adopted by

         Commission order, four days after Responsive Testimony was filed, in order to superimpose four

         rounds of sequential legal briefing and delay the en banc hearing on the merits to January 12, 2027.

         OG&E has not shown good cause for that relief. First, the premise of the Motion, that intervenors

         and PUD “injected” novel issues by proposing modifications to OG&E’s tariff, misstates the

         function of Responsive Testimony. Proposing changes to an applicant’s tariff is what responsive
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                Page 2 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         testimony is for, and the Commission routinely approves tariffs with modifications. Second,

         OG&E’s own footnote establishes that it has been on notice of alternative-supply proposals for

         large-load customers since June 26, 2026, nearly three months before it filed the Motion. Third,

         the questions OG&E frames as “threshold” legal issues are, in substance, mixed questions of law

         and fact whose answers depend on how a given option is structured, who sells energy to whom,

         and how the transactions settle in the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) Integrated Marketplace.

         Those questions cannot be resolved in the abstract before the record is complete. Fourth, the

         proposed schedule is structurally prejudicial: it assigns a brief-in-chief to the so-called “DODGE

         Proponents,” effectively shifting to intervenors and Staff a burden of proof that belongs to OG&E

         as the applicant, and it gives OG&E the last word. Finally, the resulting delay is neither “slight”

         nor harmless, and OG&E’s adequate existing remedies, including Rebuttal Testimony due October

         5, 2026, the pre-trial motions deadline, argument at hearing, and Proposed Findings of Fact and

         Conclusions of Law, make the requested relief unnecessary.


                                               II. BACKGROUND

                On June 17, 2026, OG&E filed its Application and Direct Testimony requesting approval

         of its Extra-Large Power and Light Tariff (“XLPL Tariff”), associated Terms and Conditions of

         Service for Extra Large Load Customers (“TCXLLC”), and a regulatory asset for portfolio

         optimization software costs. As OG&E acknowledges, the parties, including OG&E, negotiated a

         procedural schedule that was communicated to the ALJ on June 24, 2026, and recommended by

         the ALJ on June 25, 2026. Motion at 2 n.1. That schedule was adopted in Order No. 758969, issued

         July 9, 2026, which currently sets the Hearing on the Merits before the Commission en banc for

         November 3, 2026.
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                 Page 3 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

                  OG&E’s footnote further concedes that alternative-supply frameworks for large-load

         customers were proposed in Case No. PUD2025-000075 on June 26, 2026, one day after the ALJ

         recommended the schedule in this case and nine days after OG&E filed its Application. Id. OG&E

         devotes a paragraph of its Motion to the record in that proceeding, confirming that it has followed

         those developments closely. Motion ¶ 3. OG&E filed two separate detailed briefs (as thinly

         disguised “Public Comment”) on these very issues in the PUD2025-000075 Case. See Entries 835

         & 863.

                  On September 18, 2026, Responsive Testimony was filed. Among other things, the

         witnesses for Google, LLC, the Oklahoma Industrial Energy Consumers (“OIEC”), the Petroleum

         Alliance of Oklahoma, and PUD each addressed, in varying scope and with materially different

         content, options under which an extra-large-load customer could obtain some or all of its energy

         supply through arrangements other than OG&E’s bundled generation service. Motion ¶ 2. OG&E

         filed this Motion four days later.

                  The Motion proposes to (a) leave the Rebuttal, Sur-Rebuttal, settlement conference, and

         discovery deadlines unchanged; (b) add a “DODGE Proponents Brief-in-Chief” due October 30,

         2026, responsive briefs due November 20, 2026, reply briefs due December 4, 2026, and sur-reply

         briefs due December 18, 2026; and (c) move the pre-hearing conference, public comment, and en

         banc Hearing on the Merits to January 12, 2027, with Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions

         of Law due January 29, 2027. Motion ¶ 10.


                                                 III. ARGUMENT

         A.       OG&E Has Not Shown Good Cause to Amend a Negotiated Procedural Schedule
                  Adopted by Commission Order.

                  Order No. 758969 reflects a schedule OG&E itself negotiated and on which every party

         has since relied in allocating witness, consultant, and attorney resources. A party seeking to modify
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                 Page 4 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         such an order bears the burden of demonstrating good cause. OG&E’s good-cause showing rests

         on the proposition that alternative-supply proposals “had not been raised when the existing

         procedural schedule was developed and therefore were not anticipated.” Motion ¶ 4. That

         proposition fails for two independent reasons.

                First, nothing about the Responsive Testimony is procedurally unusual. When a utility files

         a new tariff, the Commission is not confined to approving or rejecting it as filed; it may approve

         the tariff with such modifications as it finds just and reasonable. The entire purpose of the

         Responsive Testimony phase is to allow Staff and intervenors to identify deficiencies in the

         applicant’s proposal and to recommend alternatives. Recommendations that a large-load tariff

         include an alternative-supply option are recommendations about the terms and conditions of the

         tariff under review. They are no more “injected” into this proceeding than a recommended change

         to a demand charge, a minimum-bill provision, or a collateral requirement. If every substantive

         alternative proposed in responsive testimony justified a separate round of sequential legal briefing

         and a delayed hearing, no procedural schedule in a contested tariff case could survive its

         responsive-testimony deadline.

                Second, OG&E’s claim of surprise is contradicted by its own Motion. OG&E concedes

         that alternative-supply frameworks for large-load customers were proposed in Case No. PUD2025-

         000075 on June 26, 2026. That was well before any testimony deadline in this case and nearly

         three months before OG&E filed the Motion. OG&E knew, or should have anticipated, that parties

         who advanced or supported such frameworks in the PSO large-load proceeding would advance

         similar proposals in response to OG&E’s own large-load tariff. OG&E could have sought a legal

         briefing provision at any time after June 26. It did not. It instead waited until Responsive
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                  Page 5 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         Testimony was filed and now seeks to reorder the balance of the case. A party’s strategic choice

         to wait is not good cause.

                Moreover, OG&E has adequate remedies within the existing schedule. It may address the

         legal and policy objections it identifies in Rebuttal Testimony due October 5, 2026, to which other

         parties may respond in Sur-Rebuttal Testimony due October 20, 2026. It may file pre-trial motions

         by the existing deadline. It may present legal argument at the hearing, and it may brief every one

         of the questions listed in paragraph 5 of its Motion in its Proposed Findings of Fact and

         Conclusions of Law. The existing schedule already provides a full opportunity for the Commission

         to receive “focused advocacy directed specifically to the legal issues presented.” Motion ¶ 7(e).

         B.     The Questions Identified by OG&E Are Mixed Questions of Law and Fact That
                Cannot Be Resolved Before the Evidentiary Record Is Complete.

                OG&E characterizes the eight questions in paragraph 5 of its Motion as “threshold legal

         and jurisdictional issues.” Motion ¶¶ 9, 11. Few of them are. Whether a particular arrangement

         “would permit or facilitate retail wheeling” (¶ 5(d)), whether it relies on “unauthorized/unregulated

         retail electric service under the guise of ‘wholesale-market’ transactions” (¶ 5(e)), whether it is

         consistent with the Retail Electric Supplier Certified Territory Act, 17 O.S. §§ 158.21 et seq. (¶

         5(b)), and whether it “relieve[s] the utility of any legal obligation to serve” (¶ 5(h)) are questions

         whose answers turn on the specific structure of the arrangement. Among the facts that matter are:

         which entity sells electric energy to the end-use customer at retail; whether OG&E remains the

         sole retail electric supplier to the premises within its certified territory; where and how title to

         energy passes; how the customer’s load and any associated resources are registered and settled in

         the SPP Integrated Marketplace; what capacity, resource-adequacy, ancillary, backup, and delivery

         services OG&E continues to provide and at what rates; and what cost-allocation and hold-harmless

         protections apply to other customers. Those are matters that are not at issue in this proceeding and
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                 Page 6 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         need not be resolved unless and until a contract of transaction exists that would bring these

         questions to the fore. Until such facts actually exist, it would be premature for the Commission to

         attempt to answer such questions.

                The jurisdictional line between wholesale and retail transactions, which OG&E places at

         the center of its Motion, illustrates the point. Courts and regulators draw that line by examining

         how a transaction is actually structured and where it operates, not by applying labels. See, e.g.,

         FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260 (2016); Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC,

         578 U.S. 150 (2016). Asking the Commission to decide whether an undefined category of

         “DODGE” arrangements is lawful, before the record establishes what any particular arrangement

         would entail, invites either an advisory ruling of little practical value or a premature ruling that

         forecloses options the Commission might otherwise find lawful and in the public interest once the

         facts are developed.

                The problem is compounded by OG&E’s decision to aggregate four different parties’

         proposals under a single invented acronym. The Responsive Testimony OG&E cites ranges from

         roughly one page (Dauphinais 49:1–50:9) to more than eight pages (Kimbrough 50:16–58:13), and

         the proposals differ materially in structure, scope, and the role they reserve to OG&E. A single

         “Brief-in-Chief” by the “DODGE Proponents” would require parties with differing positions to

         defend a composite framework none of them proposed. That is not issue-narrowing; it is issue-

         blurring.

                Finally, the proposed briefing would not streamline anything. Because the questions are

         fact-bound, they would have to be re-argued in Proposed Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law

         after the hearing, which the Motion retains. Motion ¶ 10. The net effect would be two full rounds
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                 Page 7 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         of legal briefing on the same issues, one of them conducted without a record, plus a delayed

         hearing. That is the opposite of judicial economy.

         C.     The Proposed Schedule Would Improperly Shift the Burden of Proof and Is
                Structurally Prejudicial.

                OG&E is the applicant. It bears the burden of proving that its XLPL Tariff, as filed or as

         modified, is fair, just, reasonable, and in the public interest. That burden includes demonstrating

         that its proposal adequately protects other customers from the costs and risks of serving extra-large

         loads, which is precisely the context in which alternative-supply options have been raised.

                The proposed schedule inverts that allocation. It requires the “DODGE Proponents” to file

         a brief-in-chief establishing the Commission’s legal authority to adopt their recommendations,

         after which OG&E responds, the proponents reply, and OG&E files a sur-reply. Motion ¶ 10. In

         practical effect, the schedule treats Staff and intervenors as though they were applicants carrying

         the burden of proof, and it gives OG&E the final word. No rule of the Commission contemplates

         that allocation, and nothing in the Motion justifies it. Four rounds of sequential briefing, with the

         applicant speaking last on the question of what modifications the Commission may make to the

         applicant’s own tariff, is not a neutral procedural device.

                The Motion’s terminology reinforces the concern. OG&E has coined the acronym

         “Delivery Only Deregulated Generation Election” or “DODGE” to describe proposals that, by

         OG&E’s own acknowledgment, vary in form (“retail wheeling, Build-Your-Own-Generation, self-

         supply, or similar proposals”). Motion at 1. The label is argumentative. It presupposes the answer

         to at least two of the questions OG&E says are in dispute, namely whether any of the proposals

         would “deregulate” generation service or permit retail competition. PUD objects to the use of that

         term in any order issued on the Motion and requests that any such order refer neutrally to

         “alternative-supply proposals” or a similar descriptor.
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                  Page 8 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

                The Motion also candidly states that the briefing is intended to affect “the scope of

         admissible evidence and testimony.” Motion ¶ 7(c); see also ¶ 6. To the extent OG&E seeks to

         exclude or limit Responsive Testimony already filed by Staff and three intervenors, the proper

         vehicle is a properly supported pre-trial motion, for which the existing schedule already provides

         a deadline, not a briefing schedule that would function as a de facto motion in limine or dispositive

         ruling on a portion of the case without satisfying the standards applicable to such relief.

         D.     The Requested Delay Is Neither “Slight” Nor Harmless.

                The Motion describes its proposal as a “slight delay in hearing-related dates.” Motion ¶ 11.

         It is not. The Motion would move the en banc Hearing on the Merits from November 3, 2026, to

         January 12, 2027, a delay of approximately 10 weeks, and would push Proposed Findings of Fact

         and Conclusions of Law to the end of January 2027. A Commission order would follow thereafter.

                That delay carries real costs. The stated purpose of the XLPL Tariff is to establish terms of

         service for extra-large-load customers that protect OG&E’s existing customers from the costs and

         risks of serving such loads. Every month that passes without a Commission-approved framework

         is a month in which large-load service requests continue to be evaluated and negotiated without

         the tariff protections the Commission is being asked to adopt, and in which prospective customers

         and the State lack regulatory certainty. The proposed schedule also imposes practical burdens that

         the Motion does not acknowledge. It places consecutive briefing deadlines across the

         Thanksgiving and year-end holiday periods and compresses the period for Proposed Findings of

         Fact and Conclusions of Law. Those burdens fall particularly heavily on PUD and other parties

         that are simultaneously litigating other large-load proceedings before the Commission. And by

         elevating the legality of alternative-supply options into a separate briefing track immediately

         before and after the October 16, 2026, settlement conference, the schedule would tend to harden
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                                  Page 9 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

         positions at the very point when the parties should be exploring whether their differences can be

         resolved.

         E.     OG&E’s Characterization of Case No. PUD2025-000075 Is Inaccurate and Provides
                No Basis for Relief in This Case.

                The Motion asserts that there was no formal legal briefing on alternative-supply proposals

         in Case No. PUD2025-000075 “due to the last-minute nature of the surprise joint stipulation filed

         by Google and PUD without the support of the applicant utility.” Motion ¶ 3. PUD disputes that

         characterization. The joint stipulation was filed on June 26, 2026, and all parties had the

         opportunity to address it through testimony, cross-examination, and argument. Non-unanimous

         stipulations are an established feature of Commission practice, and a stipulation is not rendered

         improper because the applicant utility declines to join it. In any event, the procedural history of a

         separate docket involving a different utility is not a basis for amending the schedule in this one.


         F.     Any Modification of the En Banc Hearing Date Requires Commission Action.

                Order No. 758969 designates the ALJ to preside over pretrial matters, as OG&E notes.

         Motion ¶ 8. The date of the en banc Hearing on the Merits, however, was fixed by the Commission

         itself. OG&E appears to recognize as much in asking the ALJ to “establish, or alternatively

         recommend that the Commission establish,” its proposed schedule. Motion ¶ 12. To the extent the

         ALJ is inclined to grant any portion of the Motion, PUD respectfully submits that the existing

         hearing date should not be disturbed absent a Commission order, and that the ALJ should

         recommend against doing so for the reasons stated above.
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 53 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/29/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 11

         Case No. PUD2026-000046                                                           Page 10 of 11
         PUD’s Response Objecting to OG&E’s Motion to Amend Procedural Schedule

                                              V. CONCLUSION

                WHEREFORE, the Public Utility Division respectfully requests that the Administrative

         Law Judge deny OG&E’s Motion to Amend the Procedural Schedule in Order No. 758969 to

         Include a Briefing Schedule Regarding Proposals for Alternative Electric Service Frameworks.

                                                           Respectfully submit,
